docs.title: About
docs.text:
Econometrics Made Simple is a blog about the ideas behind applied econometrics, explained in plain words.

Each post takes one idea, wraps it in a small story, and runs the numbers in EViews. The data are simulated on purpose: because we know the truth that generated them, we can see exactly when a regression gets it right and when it is fooled.

Every post ends with a question. Leave your answer in the comments, argue with me, or tell me I'm wrong.

docs.title: Does Ice Cream Drown People?
docs.text:
Here is a headline I would love to see in a newspaper: "Ice cream linked to drownings — every extra thousand litres sold costs lives." It sounds absurd. Yet the regression behind it would look perfectly respectable.

About this post

Concept: omitted variable bias · Data sheet: P1_icecream · Simulated monthly data, 2015M01–2024M12, 120 observations

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P1_icecream · EViews program

Let me show you.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Imagine a coastal district. Every month we record three things:

  • DROWN — the number of drowning incidents
  • ICECREAM — ice cream sales, in thousand litres
  • TEMP — the average maximum temperature, in °C

A keen young analyst only has the first two series. She opens EViews and types ls drown c icecream.

Dependent Variable: DROWN
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2015M01 2024M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -1.241883      0.865828     -1.434329      0.1541
ICECREAM                  0.140186      0.006832      20.51921      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.781091    Mean dependent var              15.96667
Adjusted R-squared        0.779236    S.D. dependent var              5.017504
S.E. of regression        2.357499    Akaike info criterion           4.569606
Sum squared resid         655.8208    Schwarz criterion               4.616064
Log likelihood           -272.1764    Hannan-Quinn criter.            4.588473
F-statistic               421.0379    Durbin-Watson stat              1.833329
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Look at that t-statistic: 20.5. A p-value that rounds to zero. An R-squared of 0.78. If you only read the output, you would conclude that every extra thousand litres of ice cream brings about 0.14 more drownings a month.

docs.title: What went wrong?
docs.text:
Nothing in the arithmetic. Everything in the thinking.

On hot days, people buy ice cream. On hot days, people also go swimming. Temperature drives both series. Ice cream is simply standing in for the weather, like a witness who happened to be at the scene of the crime.

Econometricians call this omitted variable bias. When a variable that matters (temperature) is left out, and it is correlated with a variable we include (ice cream), the included variable quietly absorbs its effect.

The idea fits in one line. If the true model is

\[ DROWN = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ICECREAM + \beta_2 TEMP + u \]

and we leave out TEMP, then the slope we estimate on ICECREAM is not β1. It is β1 plus (β2 × how strongly TEMP moves with ICECREAM). Two things must both be true for the bias to appear: the omitted variable must affect the outcome, and it must be correlated with the included regressor.

docs.title: Now let the weather in
docs.text:
ls drown c icecream temp

Dependent Variable: DROWN
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2015M01 2024M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -58.18576      11.26668     -5.164408      0.0000
ICECREAM                 -0.027916      0.033755     -0.827000      0.4099
TEMP                      2.506193      0.494653      5.066571      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.820479    Mean dependent var              15.96667
Adjusted R-squared        0.817410    S.D. dependent var              5.017504
S.E. of regression        2.144006    Akaike info criterion           4.387912
Sum squared resid         537.8212    Schwarz criterion               4.457599
Log likelihood           -260.2747    Hannan-Quinn criter.            4.416212
F-statistic               267.3670    Durbin-Watson stat              1.936825
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

The "ice cream effect" collapses. Its coefficient is now slightly negative and its p-value is 0.41. Temperature carries the load: each extra degree adds about 2.5 drownings a month. Notice too that the standard error on ICECREAM jumped from 0.007 to 0.034. That is because ice cream and temperature are almost the same series, which is our next clue.

ls icecream c temp

Dependent Variable: ICECREAM
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2015M01 2024M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -323.1103      7.704917     -41.93560      0.0000
TEMP                      14.40366      0.248309      58.00700      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.966119    Mean dependent var              122.7550
Adjusted R-squared        0.965832    S.D. dependent var              31.63251
S.E. of regression        5.847121    Akaike info criterion           6.386302
Sum squared resid         4034.282    Schwarz criterion               6.432760
Log likelihood           -381.1781    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.405169
F-statistic               3364.812    Durbin-Watson stat              2.212365
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Temperature explains 97% of the movement in ice cream sales. No wonder ice cream looked so "guilty" when temperature was missing.

docs.title: Confession
docs.text: I generated these data. In the true model, ice cream has zero effect on drownings. Temperature alone does the work. That is the beauty of simulation: we know the truth, so we can catch the regression lying.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: A significant t-statistic tells you that a coefficient is precisely estimated. It does not tell you that the coefficient means what you want it to mean. Before you trust a slope, ask: what else moves with my X, and also moves my Y?

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: Studies often find that people who drink a little coffee live longer than people who drink none. List three omitted variables that could create this pattern. For each, say which way it would bias the coffee coefficient. Leave your answers in the comments.

docs.title: When Two Random Walks Fall in Love
docs.text:
A cinema owner keeps a weekly index of popcorn sales. Across town, a pet shop keeps a weekly index of goldfish sold. The two businesses have never heard of each other. No customer links them. No supplier links them.

About this post

Concept: spurious regression and non-stationarity · Data sheet: P2_spurious · Simulated weekly data, 200 observations

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P2_spurious · EViews program

Now watch what a regression thinks.

ls popcorn c goldfish

Dependent Variable: POPCORN
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 200
Included observations: 200

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         32.89259      2.542950      12.93481      0.0000
GOLDFISH                  1.349260      0.060292      22.37861      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.716658    Mean dependent var              89.17085
Adjusted R-squared        0.715227    S.D. dependent var              9.995533
S.E. of regression        5.334028    Akaike info criterion           6.196040
Sum squared resid         5633.468    Schwarz criterion               6.229023
Log likelihood           -617.6040    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.209388
F-statistic               500.8024    Durbin-Watson stat              0.137310
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

A t-statistic of 22. An R-squared of 0.72. On paper, each extra point of goldfish sales comes with 1.35 points of popcorn sales. A consultant could build a whole PowerPoint deck on "cross-category demand synergies".

But I built these two series myself, completely independently. Each one is a random walk: this week's value is last week's value plus a random shock.

\[ POPCORN_t = POPCORN_{t-1} + e_t \qquad GOLDFISH_t = GOLDFISH_{t-1} + v_t \]

The shocks e and v have nothing to do with each other. The true slope is exactly zero.

docs.title: Why does this happen?
docs.text:
A random walk wanders. It has no home to return to. Over 200 weeks, it drifts up for a while, then down, then sideways, purely by chance. Two such wanderers will very often drift in the same direction for long stretches. OLS sees those long shared drifts and calls them a relationship.

The usual t-test assumes the data settle around a stable mean (they are stationary). Random walks do not. With them, the t-statistic does not follow a t distribution at all; it tends to grow as the sample gets longer. More data makes the illusion stronger, not weaker. This is the famous result of Granger and Newbold (1974), later explained in theory by Phillips (1986).

docs.title: The smoking gun in the output
docs.text:
Look at the bottom right corner: Durbin-Watson stat = 0.137. A DW near 2 means the residuals behave like fresh noise. A DW near 0 means each residual is almost a copy of the last one. The residuals are wandering too.

Granger and Newbold gave a handy rule of thumb: if the R-squared is bigger than the Durbin-Watson statistic, be suspicious. Here 0.72 is more than five times 0.137.

docs.title: The cure: look at changes, not levels
docs.text:
If the two series are truly unrelated, then this week's change in goldfish sales should tell us nothing about this week's change in popcorn sales.

ls d(popcorn) c d(goldfish)

Dependent Variable: D(POPCORN)
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2 200
Included observations: 199

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -0.082319      0.100535     -0.818813      0.4139
D(GOLDFISH)              -0.006250      0.098452     -0.063480      0.9494
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.000020    Mean dependent var             -0.081859
Adjusted R-squared       -0.005056    S.D. dependent var              1.410968
S.E. of regression        1.414530    Akaike info criterion           3.541472
Sum squared resid         394.1765    Schwarz criterion               3.574570
Log likelihood           -350.3764    Hannan-Quinn criter.            3.554867
F-statistic               0.004030    Durbin-Watson stat              1.888619
Prob(F-statistic)         0.949448
==============================================================================

The romance is over. The slope is essentially zero (p = 0.95), the R-squared is 0.00002, and the Durbin-Watson statistic is back near 2.

docs.title: A word of caution
docs.text: Differencing is not always the answer. Sometimes two trending series really are tied together over the long run, such as income and consumption. Then they are cointegrated, and throwing away the levels throws away the most interesting information. Before you regress levels on levels, test each series for a unit root (in EViews: open the series, then View → Unit Root Tests). If both have unit roots, test whether they are cointegrated before you believe the levels regression.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: Global average temperature and the number of countries with a mobile phone network both trended upward for decades. Suppose someone regresses one on the other and finds R-squared = 0.95. What two checks would you ask for before reading anything into it?

docs.title: R-squared Is Not a Report Card
docs.text:
Every econometrics teacher has met this student. They run a regression, look straight at the R-squared, and feel either proud or ashamed. 0.9 is an A+. 0.2 is a fail.

About this post

Concept: R-squared, adjusted R-squared and information criteria · Data sheet: P3_rsquared · Simulated cross-section, 40 students

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P3_rsquared · EViews program

This post is for that student.

docs.title: A simple, honest model
docs.text:
Forty students. We know each student's exam SCORE (out of 100) and the HOURS they studied in the week before the exam.

ls score c hours

Dependent Variable: SCORE
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 40
Included observations: 40

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         36.44818      3.203590      11.37729      0.0000
HOURS                     3.937217      0.436062      9.029020      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.682070    Mean dependent var              63.30000
Adjusted R-squared        0.673704    S.D. dependent var              13.18741
S.E. of regression        7.532959    Akaike info criterion           6.925160
Sum squared resid         2156.328    Schwarz criterion               7.009603
Log likelihood           -136.5032    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.955692
F-statistic               81.52321    Durbin-Watson stat              2.699434
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Each extra hour of study is worth about 3.9 marks. The true value I used to generate the data was 4. Not bad at all.

docs.title: Now let's "improve" it
docs.text:
Our ambitious student wants a higher R-squared. So they add four more variables:

  • SHOE — shoe size
  • BMONTH — month of birth (1 to 12)
  • LETTERS — number of letters in the student's first name
  • BUSWAIT — minutes spent waiting for the bus on exam morning

None of these has anything to do with the score. I generated them as pure noise.

ls score c hours shoe bmonth letters buswait

Dependent Variable: SCORE
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 40
Included observations: 40

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         44.36399      8.200577      5.409862      0.0000
HOURS                     3.956930      0.469772      8.423090      0.0000
SHOE                     -0.426822      0.845106     -0.505051      0.6168
BMONTH                   -0.350492      0.393803     -0.890019      0.3797
LETTERS                  -0.040333      0.539248     -0.074795      0.9408
BUSWAIT                  -0.078291      0.076610     -1.021945      0.3140
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.698956    Mean dependent var              63.30000
Adjusted R-squared        0.654685    S.D. dependent var              13.18741
S.E. of regression        7.749381    Akaike info criterion           7.070584
Sum squared resid         2041.799    Schwarz criterion               7.323916
Log likelihood           -135.4117    Hannan-Quinn criter.            7.162181
F-statistic               15.78809    Durbin-Watson stat              2.675735
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

The R-squared went up, from 0.682 to 0.699. Shoe size and bus waiting time "explained" more of the exam scores!

docs.title: Why R-squared can only go up
docs.text:
R-squared measures how much of the variation in Y the fitted line covers. Adding any variable, even random noise, gives OLS one more knob to turn. OLS will always use it to shave off a little more of the sum of squared residuals, which fell here from 2156.3 to 2041.8. It can never make the fit worse. So R-squared never falls when you add a regressor.

That is why R-squared is a poor judge of whether a variable belongs in the model.

docs.title: The fairer judges
docs.text:
Look at the other lines in the two tables.

Measure HOURS only HOURS + 4 junk variables Better model R-squared 0.682 0.699 Looks like junk wins Adjusted R-squared 0.674 0.655 HOURS only S.E. of regression 7.53 7.75 HOURS only Akaike info criterion 6.925 7.071 HOURS only Schwarz criterion 7.010 7.324 HOURS only

Adjusted R-squared charges a fee for every extra variable. Akaike and Schwarz do the same (smaller is better), and Schwarz charges the highest fee. Every one of them prefers the simple model.

The most direct check is to test whether the four junk variables matter jointly. In the equation window: View → Coefficient Diagnostics → Wald Test, and enter c(3)=0, c(4)=0, c(5)=0, c(6)=0.

Wald Test:
Equation: EQ02

==============================================================================
Test Statistic                 Value              df     Probability
==============================================================================
F-statistic                 0.476784         (4, 34)          0.7525
Chi-square                  1.907137               4          0.7528
==============================================================================

A p-value of 0.75. The data see no reason to keep any of them.

docs.title: The other half of the story: a low R-squared can be perfectly fine
docs.text:
What if the R-squared were 0.15? Many students would panic. They should not. Human behaviour is noisy. If you want to know how much an extra hour of study is worth, what matters is whether the slope is estimated without bias and with reasonable precision. A model can capture a true, important effect and still leave most of the variation unexplained, because many other things (sleep, luck, the questions set) also move exam scores. You will see a real example in Post 4, where the correct model has an R-squared of only 0.38.

And a very high R-squared can be a warning sign rather than a medal. Post 2 showed an R-squared of 0.72 between two series that had nothing to do with each other.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: R-squared answers one narrow question: how closely does the line hug the data in this sample? It does not tell you whether the model is right, whether the coefficients are unbiased, or whether the model will predict well tomorrow.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: Model A explains house prices with R-squared = 0.90 using 25 variables and 60 houses. Model B explains them with R-squared = 0.70 using 3 variables. You must predict the price of the next 100 houses that come on the market. Which model do you trust, and why?

docs.title: The Noisy Ruler
docs.text:
Ask a student how many hours they slept last night and you will get an answer. You will not necessarily get the truth. People round, forget, guess, and sometimes tell you what sounds respectable.

About this post

Concept: measurement error and attenuation bias · Data sheet: P4_measurement · Simulated cross-section, 150 students

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P4_measurement · EViews program

What happens to a regression when the X variable is measured with a noisy ruler?

docs.title: Two rulers, one truth
docs.text:
A college runs a small study on 150 students. For each student we have:

  • MARKS — the end-of-term mark
  • SLEEP_TRACKER — average nightly sleep in hours, measured by a wrist tracker (accurate)
  • SLEEP_SELF — average nightly sleep the student says they get, rounded to the nearest half hour (noisy)

The true rule I used to build the data: every extra hour of sleep adds 4 marks.

First, the accurate ruler. ls marks c sleep_tracker

Dependent Variable: MARKS
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 150
Included observations: 150

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         41.38483      2.723096      15.19771      0.0000
SLEEP_TRACKER             3.863301      0.405631      9.524171      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.380000    Mean dependent var              67.00933
Adjusted R-squared        0.375811    S.D. dependent var              6.514891
S.E. of regression        5.147130    Akaike info criterion           6.127999
Sum squared resid         3920.956    Schwarz criterion               6.168141
Log likelihood           -457.5999    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.144308
F-statistic               90.70983    Durbin-Watson stat              2.008383
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

An estimate of 3.86, close to the true 4. Notice the R-squared of only 0.38, even though this is the correct model.

Now the noisy ruler. ls marks c sleep_self

Dependent Variable: MARKS
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 150
Included observations: 150

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         51.88233      2.427215      21.37525      0.0000
SLEEP_SELF                2.287350      0.359979      6.354114      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.214332    Mean dependent var              67.00933
Adjusted R-squared        0.209024    S.D. dependent var              6.514891
S.E. of regression        5.794139    Akaike info criterion           6.364815
Sum squared resid         4968.663    Schwarz criterion               6.404956
Log likelihood           -475.3611    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.381123
F-statistic               40.37477    Durbin-Watson stat              2.053054
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

The effect of sleep has shrunk from about 4 to about 2.3. Still "highly significant", so nobody reading the table would notice a problem. But the estimate is wrong by more than 40%.

docs.title: Why the slope shrinks
docs.text:
The self-reported number is the truth plus some noise:

\[ SLEEP\_SELF = SLEEP\_TRUE + error \]

Part of the variation in SLEEP_SELF is real differences in sleep, which do move marks. The rest is reporting noise, which moves nothing. OLS cannot tell the two apart. It averages a real effect (4) with a fake one (0), and the result is pulled towards zero.

How much shrinkage? Roughly by the share of the variance that is real:

\[ \text{reliability} = \frac{Var(SLEEP\_TRUE)}{Var(SLEEP\_SELF)} \]

In these data the tracker's variance is 1.08 and the self-report's variance is 1.74, so the reliability is about 0.62. Multiply the true effect by it: 4 × 0.62 ≈ 2.5, close to what we got. Econometricians call this attenuation bias: noise in X attenuates, or weakens, the estimated effect.

docs.title: A twist: noise in Y is far less harmful
docs.text: If the marks had been recorded with random errors instead, the slope would still be unbiased. The extra noise would simply land in the error term, making the standard errors bigger and the R-squared smaller. Noise in Y costs you precision. Noise in X costs you the right answer.

docs.title: What can we do?
docs.text:
1. Measure better. The tracker data are the best fix of all.
  2. Use an instrument. A second, independent noisy measure (say, a roommate's report of the student's sleep) can serve as an instrumental variable. In EViews: Quick → Estimate Equation → Method: TSLS.
  3. Remember the direction. With classical noise in a single regressor, the true effect is probably larger than your estimate. That alone can change a policy conclusion.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: A small, significant coefficient does not prove the effect is small. It may be a big effect seen through a foggy window.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: Surveys often find that the measured return to an extra year of schooling is modest. Years of schooling are usually self-reported. Using this post, which way would that bias the estimate? Now think of a reason why the bias could go the other way.

docs.title: When the Errors Fan Out
docs.text:
Ask a family earning ₹20,000 a month how much they spend on food, and the answer will sit in a narrow range. There is only so much room to move. Ask a family earning ₹1,50,000 a month, and the answers spread out. One family cooks simple meals at home; another eats out four nights a week. Same income, very different food bills.

About this post

Concept: heteroskedasticity, the White test and robust standard errors · Data sheet: P5_hetero · Simulated cross-section, 200 households

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P5_hetero · EViews program

That simple observation has a long name: heteroskedasticity. It means the spread of the errors is not the same for everyone.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
For 200 households we have monthly FOOD spending and monthly INCOME, both in ₹ thousand.

ls food c income

Dependent Variable: FOOD
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 200
Included observations: 200

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         3.557278      0.839040      4.239702      0.0000
INCOME                    0.221461      0.009361      23.65894      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.738699    Mean dependent var              21.56240
Adjusted R-squared        0.737379    S.D. dependent var              9.749858
S.E. of regression        4.996469    Akaike info criterion           6.065290
Sum squared resid         4943.010    Schwarz criterion               6.098273
Log likelihood           -604.5290    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.078637
F-statistic               559.7454    Durbin-Watson stat              1.799203
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Out of every extra ₹1,000 of income, about ₹221 goes on food. That is a sensible marginal propensity to spend on food, and close to the 0.22 I used to create the data.

So far, so good. But the table has a hidden assumption. Every standard error above is computed as if the errors have the same variance for every household. We have just argued they don't.

docs.title: Picture it first
docs.text: In EViews, open the equation and choose View → Actual, Fitted, Residual → Residual Graph, or make a scatter of the residuals against INCOME. You will see a fan or a trumpet: residuals huddle close to zero for poorer households and spread wide for richer ones.

docs.title: Then test it
docs.text:
View → Residual Diagnostics → Heteroskedasticity Tests → White.

Heteroskedasticity Test: White
Null hypothesis: Homoskedasticity

==============================================================================
F-statistic               23.09812    Prob. F(2,197)                    0.0000
Obs*R-squared             37.99092    Prob. Chi-Square(2)               0.0000
Scaled explained SS       70.91685    Prob. Chi-Square(2)               0.0000
==============================================================================

The idea behind the White test is easy. Take the squared residuals, which are rough measures of each household's error variance. Regress them on INCOME and INCOME squared. If income helps predict how big the errors are, the variance is not constant. Here it clearly does: all three p-values are 0.0000. We reject homoskedasticity.

docs.title: Does it matter?
docs.text: Here is the good news, which surprises many students: the coefficients are still unbiased. Heteroskedasticity does not move the line. The bad news: the usual standard errors are wrong, so the t-statistics and p-values cannot be trusted.

docs.title: Fix 1: robust standard errors
docs.text:
Keep the same coefficients, but compute standard errors that allow the variance to differ across households. In EViews, under Options choose Covariance method: White, or type ls(cov=white) food c income.

Dependent Variable: FOOD
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 200
Included observations: 200
White heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors & covariance

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         3.557278      0.651411      5.460885      0.0000
INCOME                    0.221461      0.010455      21.18271      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.738699    Mean dependent var              21.56240
Adjusted R-squared        0.737379    S.D. dependent var              9.749858
S.E. of regression        4.996469    Akaike info criterion           6.065290
Sum squared resid         4943.010    Schwarz criterion               6.098273
Log likelihood           -604.5290    Hannan-Quinn criter.            6.078637
F-statistic               559.7454    Durbin-Watson stat              1.799203
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000

Compare the two tables line by line. The coefficients are identical. The R-squared is identical. Only the standard errors changed: the one on INCOME rose from 0.0094 to 0.0105, and the one on C fell. Robust standard errors do not always get bigger. They get honest.

docs.title: Fix 2: change the scale
docs.text:
Often the fan exists because the relationship is proportional. A rich family's errors are big in rupees but similar in percentages. Taking logs puts everyone on a percentage scale. ls log(food) c log(income)

Dependent Variable: LOG(FOOD)
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 200
Included observations: 200

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -0.125851      0.119511     -1.053048      0.2936
LOG(INCOME)               0.725762      0.027822      26.08553      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.774604    Mean dependent var              2.963323
Adjusted R-squared        0.773466    S.D. dependent var              0.477765
S.E. of regression        0.227395    Akaike info criterion          -0.114305
Sum squared resid         10.23830    Schwarz criterion              -0.081322
Log likelihood            13.43052    Hannan-Quinn criter.           -0.100957
F-statistic               680.4549    Durbin-Watson stat              1.877997
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Heteroskedasticity Test: White
Null hypothesis: Homoskedasticity

==============================================================================
F-statistic               1.722627    Prob. F(2,197)                    0.1813
Obs*R-squared             3.437601    Prob. Chi-Square(2)               0.1793
Scaled explained SS       5.581220    Prob. Chi-Square(2)               0.0614
==============================================================================

The White test no longer rejects at 5%. As a bonus, the slope now has a neat meaning: a 1% rise in income raises food spending by about 0.73%. Food is a necessity (elasticity below 1), just as Ernst Engel noticed in the 1850s.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: Heteroskedasticity is not a disaster; it is information. It tells you the world is more varied at one end than at the other. Ignore it and your p-values lie. Notice it and you often discover a better way to write the model.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: In the log model, the constant has a p-value of 0.29. Should we drop it? What would forcing the line through the origin mean economically for a family with an income of ₹1,000 a month?

docs.title: The Monsoon Dummy
docs.text:
In Kerala, nobody needs an econometrician to tell them when umbrellas sell. The southwest monsoon arrives around the start of June and stays until September. Schools reopen in early June, so late May brings a rush of parents buying umbrellas, raincoats and school bags.

About this post

Concept: dummy variables, seasonality and the dummy variable trap · Data sheet: P6_monsoon · Simulated monthly data, 2015M01–2024M12, 120 observations

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P6_monsoon · EViews program

So why write a post about it? Because umbrellas give us the cleanest possible lesson on dummy variables: variables that are simply 1 or 0, "yes" or "no".

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
A chain of shops records UMBRELLA sales (thousand units) each month. We also create:

  • TREND — 1, 2, 3, … to capture slow growth over the years
  • MONSOON — 1 in June, July, August and September; 0 otherwise
  • MAY — 1 in May (the school-reopening rush); 0 otherwise

In EViews you can make the dummies in one line each: series monsoon = @month>=6 and @month<=9 and series may = @month=5.

docs.title: Model 1: ignore the season
docs.text:
ls umbrella c trend

Dependent Variable: UMBRELLA
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2015M01 2024M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         32.60882      3.602833      9.050883      0.0000
TREND                     0.089234      0.051680      1.726686      0.0868
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.024644    Mean dependent var              38.00750
Adjusted R-squared        0.016378    S.D. dependent var              19.77291
S.E. of regression        19.61032    Akaike info criterion           8.806516
Sum squared resid         45378.64    Schwarz criterion               8.852974
Log likelihood           -526.3909    Hannan-Quinn criter.            8.825382
F-statistic               2.981444    Durbin-Watson stat              0.655093
Prob(F-statistic)         0.086841
==============================================================================

A miserable model. The R-squared is 0.02, and the trend is not even significant at 5%. The Durbin-Watson of 0.66 shouts that the residuals have a pattern. Of course they do: every June to September they are large and positive, and every other month they are negative. The season is hiding in the error term.

docs.title: Model 2: let the rain in
docs.text:
ls umbrella c trend monsoon may

Dependent Variable: UMBRELLA
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2015M01 2024M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         18.47312      0.782806      23.59859      0.0000
TREND                     0.078974      0.010393      7.598777      0.0000
MONSOON                   41.33496      0.781607      52.88456      0.0000
MAY                       11.73740      1.332950      8.805582      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.961241    Mean dependent var              38.00750
Adjusted R-squared        0.960239    S.D. dependent var              19.77291
S.E. of regression        3.942762    Akaike info criterion           5.614405
Sum squared resid         1803.263    Schwarz criterion               5.707322
Log likelihood           -332.8643    Hannan-Quinn criter.            5.652139
F-statistic               958.9549    Durbin-Watson stat              2.305910
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Now read each line like a sentence:

  • C = 18.5: in a dry month (not May, not monsoon), at the start of the sample, the shops sell about 18,500 umbrellas.
  • MONSOON = 41.3: in a monsoon month, sales are about 41,300 higher than in a dry month.
  • MAY = 11.7: May sales are about 11,700 higher than an ordinary dry month.
  • TREND = 0.079: underneath the seasons, sales grow by about 79 umbrellas a month.

See what happened to TREND. In Model 1 it was insignificant (t = 1.7). Now t = 7.6. The trend was always there. It was simply drowned out by the seasonal noise we had refused to model. Controlling for something obvious can make a subtle effect visible.

docs.title: The dummy variable trap
docs.text:
An eager student thinks: "Why not have a dummy for the dry season too?" They create series dry = 1 - monsoon and type ls umbrella c trend monsoon dry may. EViews replies:

Near singular matrix error. Regressors may be perfectly collinear.

Here is why. For every month, MONSOON + DRY = 1. And the constant C is also a column of 1s. So C is exactly equal to MONSOON + DRY. OLS is being asked to share out the same information three ways, and there is no unique answer. This is perfect multicollinearity, and it has a famous name: the dummy variable trap.

The rule: if a category has m groups, include m − 1 dummies with a constant. The group you leave out becomes the base, and every dummy coefficient is a difference from that base.

Or drop the constant and keep all m dummies: ls umbrella trend monsoon dry may

Dependent Variable: UMBRELLA
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2015M01 2024M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
TREND                     0.078974      0.010393      7.598777      0.0000
MONSOON                   59.80808      0.892846      66.98587      0.0000
DRY                       18.47312      0.782806      23.59859      0.0000
MAY                       11.73740      1.332950      8.805582      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.961241    Mean dependent var              38.00750
Adjusted R-squared        0.960239    S.D. dependent var              19.77291
S.E. of regression        3.942762    Akaike info criterion           5.614405
Sum squared resid         1803.263    Schwarz criterion               5.707322
Log likelihood           -332.8643    Hannan-Quinn criter.            5.652139
                                      Durbin-Watson stat              2.305910
==============================================================================

Same fit, same residuals, same R-squared. Only the labels changed. Now each dummy gives a level instead of a difference: 59.8 thousand in a monsoon month, 18.5 in a dry month. And 59.8 − 18.5 = 41.3, exactly the MONSOON coefficient from Model 2. (EViews drops the F-statistic here because there is no constant to test against.)

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: A dummy variable is a way of letting the intercept move. It lets the data say, "in this group, everything starts from a different level." The choice of base group is yours; the story the model tells is the same.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: The MAY dummy assumes the pre-monsoon rush is the same every year. Suppose the monsoon arrived on 22 May one year and on 8 June another. How would you change the model to let the data tell you whether an early monsoon steals sales from June or adds new ones?

docs.title: The Day the Rules Changed
docs.text:
Some dates divide history into "before" and "after". For anyone in India, 8 November 2016 is one of them. Overnight, the old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes stopped being legal tender, and millions of people who had never used a payments app suddenly had a reason to try one.

About this post

Concept: structural breaks, the Chow test and break dummies · Data sheet: P7_break · Simulated monthly data, 2012M01–2021M12, 120 observations

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P7_break · EViews program

This post is not about whether that policy was good or bad. It is about a quieter question every econometrician should ask: is the relationship I am estimating the same over the whole sample?

docs.title: The data
docs.text: DIGITAL is the percentage of retail payments in a town made digitally, recorded monthly. The numbers are simulated, but the shape will look familiar. Our only regressor is TREND (1 for 2012M01, up to 120 for 2021M12).

docs.title: A model that looks fine
docs.text:
ls digital c trend

Dependent Variable: DIGITAL
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2012M01 2021M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         3.416723      0.867505      3.938563      0.0001
TREND                     0.458773      0.012444      36.86818      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.920123    Mean dependent var              31.17250
Adjusted R-squared        0.919446    S.D. dependent var              16.63673
S.E. of regression        4.721854    Akaike info criterion           5.958806
Sum squared resid         2630.917    Schwarz criterion               6.005264
Log likelihood           -355.5284    Hannan-Quinn criter.            5.977673
F-statistic               1359.262    Durbin-Watson stat              0.639778
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

R-squared 0.92. A t-statistic of 37. The digital share grows by about 0.46 percentage points a month. Case closed?

Not quite. That Durbin-Watson of 0.64 again tells us the residuals march in long runs rather than bouncing around zero. If you plot them (View → Actual, Fitted, Residual), you see a smile: residuals are positive in 2012–13, sink to their deepest just before November 2016, stay negative into 2018, and turn positive again from 2019. One straight line is being forced through two different stories.

docs.title: The Chow test
docs.text:
Gregory Chow's idea (1960) is beautifully simple. Fit the model separately on the "before" and "after" samples. If the world did not change, the two separate fits should do no better than the single fit. If they do much better, the relationship broke.

In EViews: View → Stability Diagnostics → Chow Breakpoint Test, and enter 2016M11.

Chow Breakpoint Test: 2016M11
Null Hypothesis: No breaks at specified breakpoints
Varying regressors: All equation variables
Equation Sample: 2012M01 2021M12

==============================================================================
F-statistic               137.2203    Prob. F(2,116)                    0.0000
Log likelihood ratio      145.6423    Prob. Chi-Square(2)               0.0000
Wald Statistic            274.4407    Prob. Chi-Square(2)               0.0000
==============================================================================

An F-statistic of 137 with a p-value of 0.0000. The null of "no break" is firmly rejected. The F has 2 numerator degrees of freedom because two things were allowed to change: the intercept and the slope.

docs.title: Model the break instead of ignoring it
docs.text:
Create two new variables: series post = (trend>=59), which is 1 from November 2016 onward, and use post*(trend-59) so the new slope starts counting from the break.

ls digital c trend post post*(trend-59)

Dependent Variable: DIGITAL
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 2012M01 2021M12
Included observations: 120

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                         11.67459      0.690609      16.90477      0.0000
TREND                     0.151650      0.020361      7.448248      0.0000
POST                      7.233032      0.949379      7.618695      0.0000
POST*(TREND-59)           0.417937      0.027458      15.22120      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.976268    Mean dependent var              31.17250
Adjusted R-squared        0.975655    S.D. dependent var              16.63673
S.E. of regression        2.595829    Akaike info criterion           4.778454
Sum squared resid         781.6458    Schwarz criterion               4.871370
Log likelihood           -282.7072    Hannan-Quinn criter.            4.816187
F-statistic               1590.665    Durbin-Watson stat              2.049174
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

Now the story is clear:

Period Monthly growth in digital share What changed Before Nov 2016 0.15 points a month Slow, steady adoption At Nov 2016 One-time jump of 7.2 points The shock itself After Nov 2016 0.15 + 0.42 = 0.57 points a month Adoption almost four times faster

The single-trend model said 0.46 points a month throughout. That number described no actual period in the data. It was an average of a slow world and a fast world. The Durbin-Watson is now 2.05, and the standard error of the regression has nearly halved, from 4.72 to 2.60.

docs.title: Two cautions
docs.text:
1. Know your date before you look. The Chow test assumes you picked the break date for a reason outside the data. If you scan every possible date and pick the one with the biggest F, the usual p-values are far too optimistic. For an unknown date, use the Quandt-Andrews test (View → Stability Diagnostics → Quandt-Andrews Breakpoint Test) or the Bai-Perron multiple breakpoint tests.
  2. A break is a fact, not an explanation. The test tells you something changed in November 2016. It does not tell you why. Smartphone prices, a new app or a festival season could all line up with the same date.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: A regression that fits beautifully over ten years can still be wrong about every single one of them. Before trusting a slope, ask whether the world stayed the same long enough for one slope to make sense.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: The COVID-19 lockdown began in March 2020, inside our sample. Should we test for a second break there? If you find one, how would you decide whether it is a permanent change or a temporary blip?

docs.title: Two Friends Who Always Arrive Together
docs.text:
Anyone who has hunted for a flat in an Indian city knows the two numbers on every listing: built-up area and carpet area. Built-up area includes the walls and balcony; carpet area is the floor you can actually lay a carpet on. Carpet area is usually around three-quarters to four-fifths of built-up area.

About this post

Concept: multicollinearity, VIFs and joint tests · Data sheet: P8_multicol · Simulated cross-section, 60 flats

Download the data (Excel) — sheet P8_multicol · EViews program

Both surely matter for the rent. So let's put both in a regression and see which one matters more.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Sixty flats. For each: monthly RENT (₹ thousand), BUILTUP area and CARPET area (both in sq ft).

ls rent c builtup carpet

Dependent Variable: RENT
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 60
Included observations: 60

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -0.712800      1.395905     -0.510636      0.6116
BUILTUP                   0.006876      0.016366      0.420123      0.6760
CARPET                    0.007881      0.020938      0.376396      0.7080
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.741175    Mean dependent var              16.32833
Adjusted R-squared        0.732094    S.D. dependent var              6.147622
S.E. of regression        3.181988    Akaike info criterion           5.201596
Sum squared resid         577.1278    Schwarz criterion               5.306313
Log likelihood           -153.0479    Hannan-Quinn criter.            5.242557
F-statistic               81.61314    Durbin-Watson stat              1.837909
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

A genuine puzzle. Look at the two t-statistics: 0.42 and 0.38. Neither size measure is anywhere near significant. By the usual reading, the size of a flat does not affect its rent.

Now look at the bottom of the same table. The F-statistic is 81.6 with a p-value of 0.000000, and the R-squared is 0.74. The model as a whole explains rent very well.

So the regression is saying: "Size matters enormously. I just can't tell you which measure of size."

docs.title: What's going on
docs.text:
BUILTUP and CARPET move together almost perfectly. In these data their correlation is 0.998. To separate their effects, OLS needs flats where one is large and the other is small. There are hardly any such flats. When two regressors always arrive together, the data cannot say which one deserves the credit. That is multicollinearity.

Think of two friends who always come to your party together. Your party is always livelier when they come. But is it him or her? You will never know unless one of them turns up alone.

docs.title: Measuring the damage: VIFs
docs.text:
In EViews: View → Coefficient Diagnostics → Variance Inflation Factors.

Variance Inflation Factors
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 60
Included observations: 60

==============================================================================
                         Coefficient      Uncentered        Centered
Variable                    Variance             VIF             VIF
==============================================================================
C                           1.948551        11.54692              NA
BUILTUP                     0.000268        2973.339        257.5242
CARPET                      0.000438        2966.174        257.5242
==============================================================================

Read the Centered VIF column. A VIF of 257 means the variance of each slope is about 257 times bigger than it would be if the two regressors were unrelated. So each standard error is about √257 ≈ 16 times bigger. A common rule of thumb flags VIFs above 10. We are far beyond that.

docs.title: Asking the right question: a joint test
docs.text:
The individual t-tests ask, "Does BUILTUP matter, holding CARPET fixed?" That is a strange question; in real life you almost never change one without the other. The sensible question is, "Does size matter at all?" Test both slopes together. View → Coefficient Diagnostics → Wald Test, with c(2)=0, c(3)=0.

Wald Test:
Equation: EQ01

==============================================================================
Test Statistic                 Value              df     Probability
==============================================================================
F-statistic                 81.61314         (2, 57)          0.0000
Chi-square                  163.2263               2          0.0000
==============================================================================

Emphatically yes. Together, the two size variables are hugely significant. Each one on its own looked useless only because it was sharing the credit with its twin.

docs.title: One sensible fix
docs.text:
Keep one measure of size. ls rent c builtup

Dependent Variable: RENT
Method: Least Squares
Date: 10/27/26   Time: 21:45
Sample: 1 60
Included observations: 60

==============================================================================
Variable               Coefficient    Std. Error   t-Statistic       Prob.
==============================================================================
C                        -0.707777      1.385475     -0.510855      0.6114
BUILTUP                   0.013024      0.001012      12.86601      0.0000
==============================================================================
R-squared                 0.740532    Mean dependent var              16.32833
Adjusted R-squared        0.736058    S.D. dependent var              6.147622
S.E. of regression        3.158356    Akaike info criterion           5.170745
Sum squared resid         578.5622    Schwarz criterion               5.240557
Log likelihood           -153.1224    Hannan-Quinn criter.            5.198052
F-statistic               165.5343    Durbin-Watson stat              1.847104
Prob(F-statistic)         0.000000
==============================================================================

The standard error drops from 0.0164 to 0.0010, and the t-statistic leaps to 12.9. The R-squared barely moves (0.741 to 0.741). An extra 100 sq ft of built-up area adds about ₹1,300 a month to the rent. Both Akaike and Schwarz prefer this simpler model.

But be honest about what this coefficient now means. It is the effect of built-up area together with the carpet area that comes with it. It is not the effect of adding walls while holding the floor fixed. Dropping CARPET is fine for predicting rent. It would be wrong to claim we have isolated the separate value of a wall. Notice the link to Post 1: dropping a correlated variable always shifts its effect onto the one you keep.

docs.title: Things that do not fix multicollinearity
docs.text:
• Removing a variable just because its t-statistic is small, when theory says it belongs and it is not a near-duplicate.
  • Hoping that a fancier estimation method will create information the data do not contain.

What does help: more data with genuine variation (old buildings with thick walls, new ones with thin walls), combining the variables into one index that makes sense, or using outside information about one of the coefficients.

docs.title: The lesson
docs.text: Multicollinearity is not a mistake in your model. It is a shortage of information in your data. The coefficients are still unbiased; they are just blurry. Insignificant t-statistics alongside a highly significant F-statistic is its signature.

docs.title: Something to think about
docs.text: A researcher regresses a child's test score on both the mother's years of schooling and the father's years of schooling. Neither is significant, but the F-test is. A journalist writes: "Study finds parents' education doesn't matter." Write a two-sentence letter to the editor explaining what went wrong.
